column1: # Shared CONNECT grammar for the desktop (Rust) and Android (Kotlin) proxies.
# Consumers (both load THIS file, neither keeps its own copy of the vectors):
#       `connect vectors agree with the rust parser`       (test resource)
# Format: tab-separated, one vector per line, '#' starts a comment, blank lines
# `request` rows go through the production request-line parser
# go through the production authority parser: the whole `CONNECT <authority>
# HTTP/1.1` line on desktop, `parseAuthority` on Android. `hex` rows carry a
# complete wire head, so framing bytes and bytes a TSV column cannot express
# (bare LF, bare CR, 0xFF, NUL, 0x01, DEL, missing terminator) are decided by
# the same production entry point. Android's `readHead` decodes ISO-8859-1, so
# the test decodes these bytes the same way before calling `parseConnectHead`.
# One file rather than two keeps the shared rules in one place: a method,
# version, character, bracket, framing or port rule added to one parser alone
# `accept` means the PARSER accepts the line. It does NOT mean the destination
# is allowed: `127.0.0.1:443` parses and is then refused by the address policy,
# exactly like an ordinary page requesting loopback. `reject` means the line is
# refused before any lookup, socket or policy decision.
# Split of authority between the standard and this app (round 23):
#   * RFC 9112 §3.1   the method is case-sensitive  -> `connect` is refused
#                        `HTTP/1.2` is valid syntax but refused TOO, because
#                        this proxy implements HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 only
#   * application     the port is required and at most five digits; host is
#                     printable ASCII with no `@ / ? # \ %`; at most 253 bytes;
#                     no empty label; brackets only around a real IPv6 literal.
#                     RFC 3986 `reg-name` would also allow sub-delims and
#                     percent-encoding; both are refused on purpose.
# A literal ASCII control byte inside a target is not expressible in the
# tab-separated `request` column; the `hex` rows below carry those, and each
# RFC 9112 §2.3 — version syntax and the app's 1.0/1.1-only contract.
# Request-line shape: single SP, exactly three fields (RFC 9112 §3).
# Authority errors surface through the whole line as well.
# authorities (production authority parser on both sides)
# Numeric-looking but not valid IPv4. The CONNECT grammar accepts them as
# hostnames; the destination policy refuses them before the resolver (both
# suites pin that separately with a resolver counter).
# Round 23: the forms the desktop parser used to hand to the resolver.
# complete raw heads (hex bytes) — framing and non-printable bytes
# The parser sees exactly these bytes, including the terminator. No row below
# relies on the test appending a CRLFCRLF.
